Narrator Vira Toland, recorded in 1979, remembers the 1919 Association letter accusing nine Ostrey Hollow families of watering their milk. It split the Keddie and Brant families, and she believes tester Ansel Keddie was skimming cream and was rightly put out after the Ashlin hearing and the $3,500 settlement.
The report doesn't recommend a levy for 1908: it's the 1966 report, and it recommends six mills on the dollar for 1967, one mill less than the 1966 levy.

Narrator Effie Loomis, Association secretary 1901–1940, writing in 1941 from the minutes, sets out Article VII (patrons paid by butterfat, with the station's test governing and no appeal) and the 1925 arbitration award of $3,800 "without admission" despite "no cause established." She notes that nobody at the hearing mentioned the crate of measures the state inspector condemned at the station in June 1923.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator Ansel Keddie, the Ostrey Hollow tester, speaks in his March 1925 statement to the board and in an unsent letter from that spring. He denies taking any cream and describes his unchanging test method. His book shows 3.61 every year from 1898, but 3.80 in 1896 on borrowed glass, in the nine weeks of 1911 on a borrowed measure, and again by 1924; he can't explain the difference, and he was put out on 30 April 1925.
The day-book records the Purcell & Weare order of 14 March 1932 as $59.65 on sixty days' credit, though the listed items actually add up to $56.15.

Narrator Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, speaking to the Ordell County Historical Society in 1959, reports what she found in the 1923 crate. The station's pipettes delivered 16.72 c.c. instead of 17.6, so every test read 95% of the truth from 1897 to 1923. That cost the patrons 76,000 lb of butterfat (about $19,000, against the $3,800 award), which the Association's ledgers booked as station gain, so nobody watered milk or stole cream.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper 1905–1945, writing in 1948, explains the "station gain" line: fat received at Larrow Green in station cream always exceeded fat credited to patrons by 5¼% "as usual." He still suspects cream was taken, since one man handled the whole station alone, and he says Vose signed the sheets every year and told him to let it alone in 1916. His own figures are shaky: 44 million lb, a 3.16 average, a six-week borrowed measure, and an 1898 entry from a line he says he began in 1905.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods valued at $2.40, taking into account the small value and her clean record.

Narrator Merle Strawn, the state dairy inspector for the Ordell circuit 1907–1936, copies out his circuit books in 1936. Every visit to Ostrey Hollow found true scales and no added water, and he says he told the manager so in 1919. He first checked the station's glass with a state burette on 12 June 1923, condemned the whole crate of pipettes because they wouldn't deliver their mark, and the tests went up once new glass arrived (3.80 in 1924).
Lemma 2.1 is named the "Interleaving" lemma.

Narrator Halbert Nym, a curator writing accession notes in 1972, catalogues sixteen items from the dairy collection: the by-laws, the 1897 Ammon invoice, the test and weigh books, the crate of pipettes, the ledgers, the 1925 award, and Strawn's, Ivy's and the college's papers. His glosses contain errors, though: the two books' keepers are swapped (Keddie's test book is labelled "E. Brant"), and he says the crate was found in the Ashlin office rather than the station loft.
Ansgar Krell stayed at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks, from 3 May to 31 May 1884, at a total charge of $28.00.

Narrator Selby Vose, the Association's manager, in his 1926 annual address, defends the $3,800 award as a generous settlement of an unproved claim and stands by his 1919 circular. He argues that water went into the Ostrey Hollow cans until the Association began looking, and dismisses the 1923 condemnation of the glass as housekeeping. His account has the timeline and figures wrong: he says the rise came after the looking began and puts the 1924 average at 3.90, but the rise began in 1924, before the 1925 petition, straight after new glass replaced the condemned pipettes in 1923.

Roy Brant, Emmet Brant's son, 1955 with a 1958 postscript: his father's weigh book shows the farm's scale and the station's always agreed, so the Hollow's lower test (which Roy puts at 0.17, the same in every season) was never a weighing problem, and he covers the 1911 nine-week rise, the 1919 circular that split Emmet from his brother-in-law Ansel Keddie, and lending the book to Ivy.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for Mrs. Content Averill's confinement and mileage, which was paid in full in cash on 20 January 1906.

Rosalie Cudd, Jerome Cudd's daughter and the Alder Corners cheesemaker, writing to Ivy in 1958: four Hessel Bottom men sent their summer milk over Redlow Ridge for sixteen seasons (1915–1930), and it tested about 3.80 every year (3.78–3.82) and was never watered, since cheese would have shown it.
The man says his crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance, and he suspects the "included" temporary crown is part of that figure.

Leland Vaught, Bulletin No. 471 introduction and method (1958): the short pipette explains the low tests, because the error is proportional, precise, and can't be seen from inside the plant, and the 1911 nine-week interval acts as a natural experiment. But his body text contradicts his own conclusion. It gives 16.27 c.c. (Ivy measured 16.72), five dozen pipettes (the invoice says six), in use from 1 May 1898 (actually 1897), a 118,000 lb shortfall (the conclusion says 76,000), and 5¼% "of fat delivered" (it is 5¼% of fat credited).
The third paragraph names vermilion, the colour of Bettine Rausch's apron.

Dell Rundle, schoolteacher, jubilee pamphlet of 1939 (reprinted 1959): the valley's accepted story that cream left the station by the back door, followed by a note added in press that takes it back, because the ledger's "station gain" shows the cream arrived at the Green heavy, not light. The pamphlet also carries errors: Article VII dated 1891, the condemnation dated 12 July, 44 million lb, a $19,600 loss, Selby called the nephew, and eleven pipettes (actually nine).
Message No. 219 was 6 words long. It was charged the $0.25 minimum plus $0.60 for the connecting company, $0.85 in all.

Alonzo Frick, the arbitration chairman, writing in the Bar yearbook in 1946: the board heard three unproved theories (Vose's water, Teague's hinted cream theft, the 1908 wet-hay report), believed Keddie's denial, deplored his 30 April dismissal, and awarded $3,800 without a finding. He has several details wrong: 3.16 for 3.61, 67,000 lb for 76,000, and two sessions held at the station. His four-book exhibit list includes Strawn's 1923 notebook, so the condemnation was in the room, but the crate itself was never produced.
The locksmith Gil Anastos's dog is a bad-tempered gray terrier named Buckley.

Hobart Sill, the retired Larrow Green buttermaker, in 1934: the Hollow cream came down heavy every year, carrying more fat than the station sheet said, which fits the station-gain line. He still blames water and says the Hollow milk was truly 3.85 against Larrow Green's 3.78, at 27¢ fat. He also claims he lent his own glass for the 1896 season (the station's own came in 1897) and that about 900,000 lb came in that first part-year, a figure Nym says exists nowhere.

Nyle Grigg, the 1908 committee chairman, reprinting his report in 1919: he found no dishonesty, blamed the wet hay and "the remedy lies with the land," and claims Bulletin 214 proved him right. His letter contradicts his own report and the bulletin. It says the committee sampled "the whole of 1908" (the report says January–March), and it gives the bulletin's figure as a two-tenths winter depression (it says at most 0.05 in winter and none in summer).

Dr. Roland Kepp, veterinary surgeon, Farm Club paper of 1926: sour wet ground starves the cow of minerals and lowers the fat, so the Hollow's gap is the land's fault and "not in a building." His figures are wrong. He gives the gap as 0.21 (it was 0.19), Bulletin 214 as two tenths (it says at most 0.05 in winter and none in summer), and the 1911 borrowed measure as six weeks of summer (it was nine), and his seasonal argument ignores that the gap was the same year-round.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven, which takes your money, runs for about forty seconds and quits.

Hazel Brant (taped at Ashlin, 1981) describes the weigh book her grandfather Emmet started, and she says the Hollow's test ran a flat 0.19 low in every season because the station's glass never delivered what was marked on it, until Ivy found the crate in the loft and proved it.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta: the scarf the woman called Tuesday wears in all weathers.

Duncan Keddie, Ansel's son (writing in 1968, with a 1970 addition), sets out the family ties: Orra is Emmet Brant's full sister, Roy and Duncan are first cousins, and Hazel and Ivy are second cousins. He says Ansel suspected "something in the glass" in 1911 but only wrote a question mark, and he traces where each record went: the test book, the Brant weigh book (begun 1 Jan 1897), Strawn's notebooks, the Alder Corners book and the crate.

The jury found that Obadiah Chalmers drowned accidentally in the Colquitt Bros. mill pond on the night of 12 January 1927 after falling from the flume edge while at work, with no evidence of any other person's hand, and it recommended that a rail or footing plank be put in at that spot.

The Ashlin Chronicle (3 October 1958) reports that Bulletin 471 clears Ansel Keddie: Ivy found the condemned pipettes in the station loft, they delivered short, and the tests read low. The feature is full of errors: it calls Ivy his great-niece (she is his granddaughter), gives eleven pipettes at 16.27 c.c. (nine, at 16.72), $19,600 (it was $19,000) and $77.39 (the invoice says $77.93), calls Rosalie Cudd a niece (she is Jerome's daughter), and says the 1908 committee "sat again" in 1925. It also accuses Ammon & Sons of knowingly selling a short lot without any evidence.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840.

Junia Ammon, the firm's historian (1949), reproduces the 14 April 1897 invoice and the evasive letter of 2 July 1923, and guesses that a reground mold ran the whole lot short by an accident nobody caught. Her chapter contradicts itself twice: the invoice items add up to $77.93 but she writes $77.39, and she says the house sold nothing into Ordell County before 1900 right beside that 1897 invoice.
The sharpness example in Proposition 4.1 uses a 7-cycle, with a pendant path of length two attached to each of its vertices.

Cleve Oram (1977), son of the cream hauler, describes the road, the station and the crate under a tarp in the loft that he often touched, which sat twenty feet above two of the three 1925 sittings. He passes on his father's belief that cream went missing, though the ledger's station gain shows the cream arrived at the Green heavy, not light. He also gets several things wrong: five dozen pipettes (six), a $3,500 award ($3,800), 67,000 lb (76,000), Ivy as Hazel's "first cousin once removed" (they are second cousins) and the Keddie–Vose kinship, which Duncan Keddie denies.

Orin Falke, the county agent (1959), gives the board a numbered summary: water ruled out by lactometer, theft disproved by the 1911 nine weeks, and the short glass as the cause. A note added later withdraws his concession on hay once Bulletin 214's ≤0.05 figure arrives, and corrects Ivy to granddaughter (not great-niece). Two figures still stand wrong: the 1924 average as 3.85 (it was 3.80) and Larrow Green at 3.78.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle, the office clerk (1953), explains that the "station gain, five and a quarter per cent, as usual" line was copied every year without anyone questioning it, and that the arbitration had all four books in the room. His point is that the answer sat in plain sight. He gets three dates wrong: the station's own outfit from 1 May 1898 (it was 1897), the condemnation in '22 (it was 1923) and the award in '24 (it was 1925). He also gives an unsupported 1,100,000 lb for the first year.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal, the color of the endpapers of the collected edition that shows Halvane's diagram.

Orra Keddie, Ansel's wife, in diary extracts from 1897–1930 published in 1964, confirms that the station's own glass arrived on 1 May 1897, ending the borrowing from Larrow Green, and records the broken measure of 8 May 1911. She describes Ansel carrying the 1919 circular door to door, Emmet's ten-year estrangement from Ansel that followed, and Ansel's dismissal and death with no one ever naming the charge. Her two slips are "eleven families" (the circular went to nine) and "four men" (the 1908 committee was three).
The Wren's Bend bridge collected $13.88 in tolls for the week of June 5–11, 1899, and the daily figures add up to that. The $6.00 in resident passes was entered separately and is not part of it.
